titleStmt.title: Statement Made by Sir John Hay on April 16th as Chairman of Meeting of a Coordinating Committee of Trade Which Has Been Set Up in London, Comprising Members of International Rubber Regulation Committee, Rubber Growers Association and Rubber Trade Association

div.head: Statement Made by Sir John Hay on April 16th as Chairman of Meeting of a Coordinating Committee of Trade Which Has Been Set Up in London, Comprising Members of International Rubber Regulation Committee, Rubber Growers Association and Rubber Trade Association

list.item: The United States Government is providing all shipping for transporting rubber from British ports in the Far East to America.

The shipping space is being allocated in America on the basis of one-third to Rubber Reserve Company and two-thirds to industry—each of the big five will get their allocation direct and smaller consumers will be handled in bulk through the medium of American Rubber Trade Association. Basis of allocation will be flexible. Mr. Viles has promised me that attention will be paid to any reasonable representations made through me regarding its practical application and that on basis of any such representations he will be prepared to consider revision.
This method of allocation should be accepted and should not be condemned in advance. I have good reason to believe that His Majesty’s Government would not lend their support to any contrary action.

Rubber Reserve Company has undertaken to buy on godown terms at upper unit of price range and endeavour is being made to agree to exact godown equivalent of this upper unit in currencies of Straits Settlements, Netherlands East Indies, Ceylon. Producers have a clear obligation under agreements concluded between the International Rubber Regulation Committee and Rubber Reserve Company to be free sellers within the price range, and all available rubber must be offered to them freely at the agreed price.
Free flow of rubber to America under the agreements is a matter of extreme urgency at the present time to which His Majesty’s Government attach the greatest importance.

I have gathered from conversations with Departments concerned that unless rubber does go out under conditions outlined above they
will feel compelled to consider very seriously taking action to ensure that it does so. Market would in that event lose that freedom which it has enjoyed since the beginning of the war.

The substance of this statement which I have just made will be telegraphed to the Governor of the Straits Settlements so that he can transmit it to the Rubber Section of Singapore Chamber of Commerce.
